# One City for the Big Sandy

> A citizen-led, evidence-based case for phased municipal consolidation in the Pikeville–Prestonsburg corridor of Eastern Kentucky: merging Coal Run Village into Pikeville, growing along the US-23/US-460 corridor through consent-based annexation, and, on a long horizon, uniting Pikeville and Prestonsburg into one regional city of more than 14,000 people spanning Pike and Floyd counties.

Key facts (verified against primary sources; see /sources):
- Pike County, KY: 65,024 people (2010) → 58,669 (2020), projected 47,928 by 2050 (−26.3% from 2010). Floyd County: 39,451 → 35,942, projected 27,400 (−30.5%). Actual 2020 counts came in below projections; the decline is running ahead of schedule.
- The legal path is a ladder under Kentucky law: interlocal shared-services agreements (KRS 65.210–65.300, cross-county allowed) → consent-based annexation of unincorporated corridor territory (KRS 81A.420; since the 2024 amendment, a 51% petition by residents or property owners cancels an annexation outright) → merger of contiguous cities by majority referendum in each city (KRS 81.410–81.440). Multi-county Kentucky cities are lawful (KRS 81A.415).
- The argument is bargaining power, not budget cuts: academic research (Leland & Thurmaier, 2010) finds no systematic evidence that consolidation reduces costs, so this site does not promise savings. It argues a unified city of more than 14,000 competes for grants, bond ratings, employers, and flood-recovery dollars in a way three separate towns of 1,700 to 7,700 cannot.
- Precedents: Lexington–Fayette merged in 1972 (69.8% yes vote); Louisville–Jefferson County merged in 2003 in explicit response to population and tax-base decline. Honesty: nationally, only ~15% of consolidation referendums pass, and opposition from any affected city government is usually fatal, which is why this site is a coalition-building tool, with voters in each city holding the final say.
- The corridor communities, south to north along US-23: Pikeville, Coal Run Village, Broad Bottom, Harold, Betsy Layne, Stanville, Ivel, Dwale, Allen, and Prestonsburg.
- The corridor is the spine, not the boundary. Communities in any direction have the same consent-based path to join if their residents choose: south on US-23 (Shelbiana, Millard, Elkhorn City), down KY-122 (Robinson Creek, Virgie), or north toward Paintsville. Elkhorn City, as an incorporated city, would require contiguity plus its own majority referendum, the same as Prestonsburg.

- Verified city data (2020 Census, KY DOR 2025 rate book, KY DOI 2025-2026 schedule, Pikeville FY2024 audit): populations Pikeville 7,754, Prestonsburg 3,681, Coal Run Village 1,669, Betsy Layne CDP 651, Dwale CDP 239, Allen 182 (verified corridor total 14,176 per the 2020 PL 94-171 file; Broad Bottom, Harold, Stanville, and Ivel have no place-level Census counts, and the county division covering that stretch records 4,601 people, so the true corridor population exceeds the 14,176 floor). Real property tax per $100: Coal Run Village 0¢, Pikeville 14.6¢, Prestonsburg 21¢, Allen 23¢. Insurance premium tax: Pikeville 0% (none on file), Coal Run 4%, Allen 6%, Prestonsburg 8%. Pikeville's General Fund (~$22.5M FY2024) is funded ~57% by its 2% occupational tax ($12.2M) versus $1.1M from property taxes; debt $31.8M; CERS net pension liability $12.1M.
- School districts are unaffected by city boundary changes under Kentucky law: KRS 160.045 (separate 75%-petition/board transfer process), KRS 160.020 (independent district registry), and Thomas v. Spragens (1948). Pikeville Independent, Pike County, and Floyd County districts would continue unchanged.
